newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries close higher as payrolls drive mkt.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries close higher as payrolls drive mkt.

text.p: The prices of U.S. Treasury securities closed higher Friday as market players breathed a sigh of relief following the release of January nonfarm payrolls data that weren't as strong as some analysts feared.

Yields on the 30-year bond sank as low as 6.67 percent within half and hour of the data release, after soaring more than a full point. As short positions were covered, the market met technical resistance and later lost some ground on comments made by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin.
The 30-year long bond ended 23/32 higher at 97-13/32.
Rubin said he supported the U.S. dollar but that it had been strong "for some time now." Some read that as a subtle shift in the administration's strong dollar policy.

"We saw a one-third retracement (after Rubin spoke) and just kept going through stops after breaking through 122-12 support in the March bond contract," said Chris Rupkey, economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.

Also pressuring bonds was news that U.S. reserve assets fell $6.89 billion in January to $68.2 billion and that U.S. holdings of foreign currencies dropped to $32.99 billion from $38.29 billion in December.
Rupkey dismissed those concerns, however.

"Reserve assets dropped because the Treasury got back some of its pesos and foreign currency holdings went down because of the dollar's strength in January," Rupkey said. "Mexico simply repaid some of its loan."

Rupkey said the foundations of the early rally were shaky to begin with. "Most of the rally occurred within 60 seconds of the headline and analysts were struggling to see why bonds were up so much," he said.
"People didn't look at this number and come in off the streets to buy bonds," Rupkey said.

"The rally was really just relief trade that the number wasn't as high as some forecasters thought it would be. But there was nothing moderate about the report, it can't be described as anything but strong," said Mark Vitner, economist in the capital markets group at First Union Corp.
Vitner said manufacturing payrolls rose for the fourth consecutive month and any damping effect weather may have had would be only temporary.
"We still think the economy's going to slow and that the data will start to show that over the next couple of months," Vitner said. "Unfortunately this number doesn't show that."
Vitner said market attention was now turning toward the Group of Seven Industrialized Nations (G-7) meeting in Berlin over the weekend.

"The G-7 meeting will be very important and I think it will be very positive for the dollar," Vitner said. "They'll release a communique that at the very least will reinforce the fact that a stronger dollar is exactly what the world needs right now."
He said a stronger dollar will moderate U.S. economic growth and help struggling economies in Europe and Japan regain their footings.
Kevin Flanagan, economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc., said cooler heads should soon prevail on the jobs data.
"This was not a weak release by any stretch of the imagination. Earnings rose only one cent, but there was no retracement in the 15-cent gain seen in November and December," Flanagan said.

Also on Friday, the two-year note ended up 4/32 at 100-2/32 and yielded 5.84 percent; the five-year closed 10/32 higher at 100-14/32 and yielded 6.15 percent, and the 10-year note closed up 15/32 at 100-23/32 to yield 6.40 percent.
(( -- N.A. Treasury desk. 212-859-1663 ))
